title: The case for export controls has retreated all the way down to a single premise that still holds
dek: First it was about preventing military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.
why: A three-hour debrief on a China trip; the second half's analysis of the policy machinery toward China — the drift in the rationale for controls, the risk of decoupling, and the alternatives — is more worth hearing than the first half's travelogue.
who: Founders, investors and teams going overseas who need to judge where US-China AI policy is heading, especially anyone assessing export controls, decoupling and open-model risk.
skip: 1:46:03–2:06:00, the segment on America's own advantages, can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: What the China discourse lacks is a target state
points.body: Nathan says the missing piece in America's discussion of China is a ‘target state’: everyone jumps straight to ‘we want to win’, but nobody answers what winning looks like, what happens if we lose, or whether there is an achievable condition for victory. The goal he offers is Pax Machina, or better, Pax Robotica — the two countries and the world sharing the prosperity and peace of the AI era, robots into factories, into fields, into homes, while avoiding the AI version of the sword of Damocles. He says explicitly that this is not about winning, it is about arriving together. A competition with no target state leaves nothing but escalation itself.

points.h: China isn't rising, it's returning to historical normal
points.body: To the claim that ‘China can't innovate’, Nathan applies one word: cope, and says it is isomorphic to cope in the AI field — conceding that AI has gotten this far, but insisting it won't reason, won't discover new knowledge, won't change paradigms. His judgment is that China's return is the long-run historical norm, and that the stretch he and Dario grew up in — China down, America the sole superpower — was the anomaly. So any effort to slow China's progress can at best work short-term, and China will be a first-tier player in nearly every major human domain. This is not a prediction, it is, in his view, something already locked in by historical structure.

points.h: On purchasing power, China is half again as big as the US
points.body: In dollar-denominated GDP, the US is about 30 trillion and China about 20 trillion, so the US is 50% bigger; on purchasing power parity, China is about 45 trillion and the US still 30 trillion, so China is 50% bigger the other way. Nathan says a good meal for two in Shanghai can come in under $10, which you can't do in New York, San Francisco or even Detroit, so the PPP measure is closer to reality. A more concrete picture: a roughly 45-minute pedicure costs about $12, and the young employee in her twenties at the shop pulls out an iPhone 17 — the iPhone 17 is not cheaper in China than in the US, and high-end Xiaomi and Huawei phones approach a thousand dollars. His explanation is the one-child structure concentrating the wealth of four grandparents plus two parents onto a single person.

points.h: The chip ban pokes at a century of humiliation
points.body: China sees itself as a top-tier civilisation that spent most of history at the technological frontier, and the one time it missed, it was invaded, opium was forced on it, and the European powers and Japan were all perpetrators — and someone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier: ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion under this framework: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already proven that the US listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script replayed: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the ban comes first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone, it has seeped into educated society; he also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

points.h: China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
points.body: Nathan did not hear a single person the whole trip say China is ahead, that China will win, and almost nobody even framed AI as a race; what he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an aging population. In a mall he asked a car-selling company about autonomous driving, and they volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, the first line of Xi Jinping's speech was that this field of AI began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left it out, and careful observers said that was an olive branch; another line was that we should jointly oppose ‘over-extending the concept of national security in the AI field’. The hardest signal China has put out so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic positioning, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

points.h: The rationale for export controls keeps retreating
points.body: Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but the effect is mostly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy's rationale: first it was preventing military applications, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, and now it has retreated to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like trying to suppress the Chinese public, so that Chinese companies and individuals can't use the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and whoever gets there first takes all — and that is basically Anthropic's belief, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory: he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan concedes he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

points.h: The most dangerous part of decoupling is not understanding each other
points.body: He asked his Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘it's not time yet’; when would it be time? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do our own thing entirely.’ From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags along a hardware-algorithm co-design fork, and add to that China stopping open weights and stopping publishing in English, and it may not take long to reach ‘we don't know the shape, the architecture, the capabilities of each other's AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely be right to panic, and genuinely right to race.

points.h: Replace the arms race with a disease gold-medal table
points.body: He first lays down a rule: don't train LLMs to maximise money-making on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training by hand the very takeover we fear most. The alternative is a ‘disease-cure gold-medal table’: both China and the US love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this would take very little capital to catalyse and could be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.
